| TriviaQA | 0.862      | 0.752    | -11.6%        | 0.737      | 0.766    | 3.9%          |
| HotpotQA | 0.324      | 0.384    | 18.5%         | 0.277      | 0.394    | 42.2%         |
| CoNaLa   | 0.226      | 0.357    | 58.0%         | 0.226      | 0.190    | -15.9%        |
| DS1000   | 0.367      | 0.353    | -3.8%         | 0.166      | 0.084    | -50.6%        |
| PNE      | 0.784      | 0.778    | -0.8%         | 0.605      | 0.629    | 4.0%          |

\# 4.2 Results and Discussion The correctness (has answer for QA tasks and pass\@1 for code tasks), as well as the confidence of RAG systems under different document types are respectively displayed in Figure 4&5.  Distracting documents degrade RAG system performance.  RAG systems incorporating distracting documents (second column in each sub-figure of Figure 4) display the poorest correctness across all datasets and models.  Since irrelevant are supposed to have minimal influence on RAG systems outputs due to their lack of useful information, the superior performance of RAG systems with irrelevant documents compared to those with distracting documents in most scenarios highlights the negative impact of the latter.  The retrieval phase of RAG systems outputs the information and materials relevant to the query, which we refer to as retrieved documents in this study.  These retrieved documents are the central component determining the effectiveness of the retrieval phase, with all advanced techniques in this phase primarily aiming to enhance their quality.  Consequently, our first research focus is on understanding the impact of retrieved document quality on the overall RAG systems.  Specifically, in our first research question (RQ1), we examine Retrieval Document Type as a key aspect of retrieved document quality.  # 4.1 Experimental Setup Retrieved documents can be classified into two main categories: oracle documents and distracting documents.  Oracle documents contain part or all of the necessary knowledge required for problem-solving, whereas distracting documents, although deemed highly similar to the problem by the retriever, do not contain useful knowledge.  To examine the impact of the retrieval document type, we introduce a third category: irrelevant documents.  These documents neither contain useful information nor exhibit high similarity to the problem.  We define three types of irrelevant documents: random (arbitrarily selected from the same knowledge base), diff (from a different domain, e.g., Wikipedia articles for a code generation task), and dummy (composed of meaningless word combinations).  To ensure a fair comparison, we keep the number of documents and the token length per document consistent.  This setup mitigates the effect of document type, allowing accurately assessing its impact on RAG system performance.  # 4.3 Follow-up Experiments: The effect of irrelevant documents Motivated by the intriguing phenomenon that RAG systems with irrelevant documents outperform those with oracle documents, we conduct additional experiments to study a follow-up question to RQ1:

Consequently, our first research focus is on understanding the impact of retrieved document quality on the overall RAG systems.  Specifically, in our first research question (RQ1), we examine Retrieval Document Type as a key aspect of retrieved document quality.  # 4.1 Experimental Setup Retrieved documents can be classified into two main categories: oracle documents and distracting documents.  Oracle documents contain part or all of the necessary knowledge required for problem-solving, whereas distracting documents, although deemed highly similar to the problem by the retriever, do not contain useful knowledge.  To examine the impact of the retrieval document type, we introduce a third category: irrelevant documents.  These documents neither contain useful information nor exhibit high similarity to the problem.  We define three types of irrelevant documents: random (arbitrarily selected from the same knowledge base), diff (from a different domain, e.g., Wikipedia articles for a code generation task), and dummy (composed of meaningless word combinations). What is the effect of irrelevant documents on code generation for LLMs and RAG systems?  We investigate this question from two perspectives: 1) Extent of Improvement: To what extent can irrelevant documents boost the code generation capabilities of LLMs and RAG systems?  2) Characteristics of Effectiveness: What are the characteristics of this effectiveness, and how does it compare to previously observed effects?  Understanding these aspects will shed light on how irrelevant documents impact RAG systems performance and may uncover new strategies for optimizing code generation in LLMs and RAG systems.  Therefore, we hypothesize two possible explanations for this effect: 1) combining irrelevant documents with retrieved documents may amplify RAG performance, as suggested by \[53], and 2) extending the input length could improve LLM performance, as indicated by \[54].  Based on these hypotheses, we design the following experiments.  Specifically, we define four initial settings: RAG systems with oracle, distracting, retrieved top-5 documents, and standalone LLMs with no documents, using the same configuration as described in Section 4.1.  These initial settings are then augmented with three types of irrelevant documents — random, diff, and dummy — as detailed in Section 4.1.  To explore the characteristics of the effectiveness of irrelevant documents, we introduce a new document type, ellipsis, consisting solely of ellipses.  Additionally, we include two control groups: 1) augmenting the initial RAG systems by repeating their original documents, referred to as repeat, and 2) using RAG systems with only irrelevant documents.  In all augmented LLMs and RAG systems, we maintain a consistent prompt length of 4000 tokens to ensure that the variations in results are not influenced by prompt length differences.  The effect of irrelevant documents resembles a "magic word" effect.

What is the effect of irrelevant documents on code generation for LLMs and RAG systems?  We investigate this question from two perspectives: 1) Extent of Improvement: To what extent can irrelevant documents boost the code generation capabilities of LLMs and RAG systems?  2) Characteristics of Effectiveness: What are the characteristics of this effectiveness, and how does it compare to previously observed effects?  Understanding these aspects will shed light on how irrelevant documents impact RAG systems performance and may uncover new strategies for optimizing code generation in LLMs and RAG systems.  Therefore, we hypothesize two possible explanations for this effect: 1) combining irrelevant documents with retrieved documents may amplify RAG performance, as suggested by \[53], and 2) extending the input length could improve LLM performance, as indicated by \[54].  Based on these hypotheses, we design the following experiments. Additionally, we include two control groups: 1) augmenting the initial RAG systems by repeating their original documents, referred to as repeat, and 2) using RAG systems with only irrelevant documents.  In all augmented LLMs and RAG systems, we maintain a consistent prompt length of 4000 tokens to ensure that the variations in results are not influenced by prompt length differences.  The effect of irrelevant documents resembles a "magic word" effect. Therefore, we hypothesize two possible explanations for this effect: 1) combining irrelevant documents with retrieved documents may amplify RAG performance, as suggested by \[53], and 2) extending the input length could improve LLM performance, as indicated by \[54]. What is the effect of irrelevant documents on code generation for LLMs and RAG systems?  We investigate this question from two perspectives: 1) Extent of Improvement: To what extent can irrelevant documents boost the code generation capabilities of LLMs and RAG systems?  2) Characteristics of Effectiveness: What are the characteristics of this effectiveness, and how does it compare to previously observed effects?  Understanding these aspects will shed light on how irrelevant documents impact RAG systems performance and may uncover new strategies for optimizing code generation in LLMs and RAG systems.  Therefore, we hypothesize two possible explanations for this effect: 1) combining irrelevant documents with retrieved documents may amplify RAG performance, as suggested by \[53], and 2) extending the input length could improve LLM performance, as indicated by \[54].  Based on these hypotheses, we design the following experiments.  Specifically, we define four initial settings: RAG systems with oracle, distracting, retrieved top-5 documents, and standalone LLMs with no documents, using the same configuration as described in Section 4.1.  These initial settings are then augmented with three types of irrelevant documents — random, diff, and dummy — as detailed in Section 4.1.  To explore the characteristics of the effectiveness of irrelevant documents, we introduce a new document type, ellipsis, consisting solely of ellipses.  Additionally, we include two control groups: 1) augmenting the initial RAG systems by repeating their original documents, referred to as repeat, and 2) using RAG systems with only irrelevant documents.  In all augmented LLMs and RAG systems, we maintain a consistent prompt length of 4000 tokens to ensure that the variations in results are not influenced by prompt length differences.  The effect of irrelevant documents resembles a "magic word" effect.  We propose that the impact of irrelevant documents presents a novel effect, which we term the "magic word" effect, based on the following observations: 1) the lack of improvement from augmenting RAG systems with ellipsis documents, repeating original documents, or extending the length of irrelevant documents suggests that the enhancement is not merely due to longer prompts, as emphasized by \[54]; and 2) the superior performance of RAG systems using only irrelevant documents, compared to those using combinations of irrelevant and retrieved documents, challenges the findings of \[53], which suggested that irrelevant documents enhance system accuracy when...

\# 5 RQ2: RETRIEVAL RECALL In this research question, we consider another critical dimension in RAG systems: Retrieval Recall.  Retrieval recall quantifies the proportion of oracle documents retrieved and utilized by RAG systems over the total oracle documents, providing an overall measure of retrieved document quality.  Given its critical role in determining RAG system performance \[19] and the observation that vanilla RAG systems often underperform compared to standalone LLMs (Section 3.5), we aim to quantify the influence of retrieval recall on RAG systems performance and determine the threshold retrieval recall required for RAG systems to surpass standalone LLMs across different datasets and models.  # 5.1 Experimental Setup To investigate the impact of retrieval recall, we first configure RAG systems with only oracle documents for each sample, representing a scenario with perfect retrieval recall.  We then control the retrieval recall to different levels: 0.8, 0.6, 0.4, 0.2, and 0, observing the corresponding performance changes in RAG systems.  To ensure a controlled setup, we maintain consistency in the number of documents and prompt token length across all retrieval recall levels.  This is achieved by randomly replacing a portion of the oracle documents with distracting documents, simulating scenarios with varying degrees of retrieval recall.  # 5.2 Results and Discussion The performance (correctness, confidence) of RAG systems under varying levels of retrieval recalls are shown in Figure 6&7.  We further summarize the retrieval recall requirements for different datasets and models in Table 5.  Correctness increases with retrieval recall.  In Figure 6, an upward trend is observed between retrieval recall and correctness across all QA datasets, as well as the code datasets CoNaLa and PNE.  However, for DS1000, while the trend is positive, notable fluctuations occur.  This is likely due to the complexity of problems in DS1000, as highlighted in Table 6.

\# 5 RQ2: RETRIEVAL RECALL In this research question, we consider another critical dimension in RAG systems: Retrieval Recall. \# 5 RQ2: RETRIEVAL RECALL In this research question, we consider another critical dimension in RAG systems: Retrieval Recall. \# 5 RQ2: RETRIEVAL RECALL In this research question, we consider another critical dimension in RAG systems: Retrieval Recall.  Retrieval recall quantifies the proportion of oracle documents retrieved and utilized by RAG systems over the total oracle documents, providing an overall measure of retrieved document quality. We then control the retrieval recall to different levels: 0.8, 0.6, 0.4, 0.2, and 0, observing the corresponding performance changes in RAG systems.  To ensure a controlled setup, we maintain consistency in the number of documents and prompt token length across all retrieval recall levels.  This is achieved by randomly replacing a portion of the oracle documents with distracting documents, simulating scenarios with varying degrees of retrieval recall.  # 5.2 Results and Discussion The performance (correctness, confidence) of RAG systems under varying levels of retrieval recalls are shown in Figure 6&7.  We further summarize the retrieval recall requirements for different datasets and models in Table 5.  Correctness increases with retrieval recall. However, for DS1000, while the trend is positive, notable fluctuations occur.  This is likely due to the complexity of problems in DS1000, as highlighted in Table 6.

\# 5 RQ2: RETRIEVAL RECALL In this research question, we consider another critical dimension in RAG systems: Retrieval Recall.  Retrieval recall quantifies the proportion of oracle documents retrieved and utilized by RAG systems over the total oracle documents, providing an overall measure of retrieved document quality. We then control the retrieval recall to different levels: 0.8, 0.6, 0.4, 0.2, and 0, observing the corresponding performance changes in RAG systems.  To ensure a controlled setup, we maintain consistency in the number of documents and prompt token length across all retrieval recall levels.  This is achieved by randomly replacing a portion of the oracle documents with distracting documents, simulating scenarios with varying degrees of retrieval recall.  # 5.2 Results and Discussion The performance (correctness, confidence) of RAG systems under varying levels of retrieval recalls are shown in Figure 6&7.  We further summarize the retrieval recall requirements for different datasets and models in Table 5.  Correctness increases with retrieval recall.  In Figure 6, an upward trend is observed between retrieval recall and correctness across all QA datasets, as well as the code datasets CoNaLa and PNE.  However, for DS1000, while the trend is positive, notable fluctuations occur.  This is likely due to the complexity of problems in DS1000, as highlighted in Table 6.

\# 5 RQ2: RETRIEVAL RECALL In this research question, we consider another critical dimension in RAG systems: Retrieval Recall. \# 5 RQ2: RETRIEVAL RECALL In this research question, we consider another critical dimension in RAG systems: Retrieval Recall.  Retrieval recall quantifies the proportion of oracle documents retrieved and utilized by RAG systems over the total oracle documents, providing an overall measure of retrieved document quality.  Given its critical role in determining RAG system performance \[19] and the observation that vanilla RAG systems often underperform compared to standalone LLMs (Section 3.5), we aim to quantify the influence of retrieval recall on RAG systems performance and determine the threshold retrieval recall required for RAG systems to surpass standalone LLMs across different datasets and models.  # 5.1 Experimental Setup To investigate the impact of retrieval recall, we first configure RAG systems with only oracle documents for each sample, representing a scenario with perfect retrieval recall.  We then control the retrieval recall to different levels: 0.8, 0.6, 0.4, 0.2, and 0, observing the corresponding performance changes in RAG systems.  To ensure a controlled setup, we maintain consistency in the number of documents and prompt token length across all retrieval recall levels.  This is achieved by randomly replacing a portion of the oracle documents with distracting documents, simulating scenarios with varying degrees of retrieval recall.  # 5.2 Results and Discussion The performance (correctness, confidence) of RAG systems under varying levels of retrieval recalls are shown in Figure 6&7.  We further summarize the retrieval recall requirements for different datasets and models in Table 5.  Correctness increases with retrieval recall.  In Figure 6, an upward trend is observed between retrieval recall and correctness across all QA datasets, as well as the code datasets CoNaLa and PNE.  However, for DS1000, while the trend is positive, notable fluctuations occur.  This is likely due to the complexity of problems in DS1000, as highlighted in Table 6.

The larger number of oracle documents and higher problem complexity may make it challenging for LLMs to establish clear relationships between the retrieved documents and the problem, thereby diminishing the effectiveness of increased retrieval recall.  Higher retrieval recall aligns with higher confidence in QA tasks but not in code tasks.  In Figure 7, perplexity decreases (confidence increases) with higher retrieval recall in QA datasets, reflecting a clear inverse relationship between retrieval recall and system confidence.  However, this trend is inconsistent in code tasks, as seen with CodeLlama-13B on CoNaLa at 0.8 retrieval recall and GPT-3.5 on DS1000 at 0.6 retrieval recall.  This suggests that perplexity may serve as a useful indicator for detecting retrieval recall quality in QA tasks when direct evaluation is challenging; however, it is not a reliable metric for code tasks.  Retrieval recall requirements range widely, from 20% to 100%.  As shown in Table 5, the minimum retrieval recall required for RAG systems to outperform corresponding standalone LLMs varies dramatically, ranging from 0.2 to 1.0 across different models and datasets.  Some datasets benefit from moderate levels of retrieval recall, while others demand near-perfect recall to achieve similar improvements. This suggests that perplexity may serve as a useful indicator for detecting retrieval recall quality in QA tasks when direct evaluation is challenging; however, it is not a reliable metric for code tasks. The larger number of oracle documents and higher problem complexity may make it challenging for LLMs to establish clear relationships between the retrieved documents and the problem, thereby diminishing the effectiveness of increased retrieval recall.  Higher retrieval recall aligns with higher confidence in QA tasks but not in code tasks.  In Figure 7, perplexity decreases (confidence increases) with higher retrieval recall in QA datasets, reflecting a clear inverse relationship between retrieval recall and system confidence.  However, this trend is inconsistent in code tasks, as seen with CodeLlama-13B on CoNaLa at 0.8 retrieval recall and GPT-3.5 on DS1000 at 0.6 retrieval recall.  This suggests that perplexity may serve as a useful indicator for detecting retrieval recall quality in QA tasks when direct evaluation is challenging; however, it is not a reliable metric for code tasks.  Retrieval recall requirements range widely, from 20% to 100%.  As shown in Table 5, the minimum retrieval recall required for RAG systems to outperform corresponding standalone LLMs varies dramatically, ranging from 0.2 to 1.0 across different models and datasets.  Some datasets benefit from moderate levels of retrieval recall, while others demand near-perfect recall to achieve similar improvements. Higher perplexity reflects lower confidence.  Guideline-3: Perplexity can be an effective and low-cost metric for evaluating retrieval quality, particu- larly in QA tasks.  Guideline-4: An RAG system may not bring benefits # 6.1 Experimental Setup In our experiments, we test different configurations for code generation and QA datasets: For code tasks, we evaluate the impact of appending top-1/5/10/15/20 retrieved docu- ments.  For QA datasets, we follow the same configuration— top-1/5/10/15/20—on Llama2-13B, with additional tests for appending top-40/60/80 documents.  This setup examines the minimum to the maximum number of docu- ments within the token limits of the models.  (GPT-3.5 and CodeLlama-13B support up to 16k tokens, while Llama2-13B has a 4k token limit.)  # 6 RQ3: DOCUMENT SELECTION As discussed in Section 2, RAG systems typically utilize pre- trained and frozen LLMs for answer generation, making the quality of the prompt the primary decisive factor in this phase.  In this research question, we first investigate the impact of document selection.  Since only a limited subset of the highest-ranked documents, as determined by the retriever, can be incorporated into the prompt, select- ing the optimal number of documents involves a crucial yet underexplored trade-off: while adding more documents increases the likelihood of including useful information, it also raises the risk of introducing distracting content that could mislead the LLM.  # 6.2 Results and Discussion The performance data is illustrated in Figure 8&9.  Confidence does not reflect correctness as the number of documents varies, especially in code tasks.  We observe inconsistencies between correctness and confidence (measured by perplexity).  As more documents are included, in QA tasks, the perplexity of RAG systems first slightly de- creases and then increases, yet correctness does not exhibit.

Confidence does not reflect correctness as the number of documents varies, especially in code tasks.  We observe inconsistencies between correctness and confidence (measured by perplexity).  As more documents are included, in QA tasks, the perplexity of RAG systems first slightly de- creases and then increases, yet correctness does not exhibit.

Fig.  10: Retrieval recall of RAG systems with varying numbers of documents.  A corresponding decline.  In code tasks, perplexity remains stable or even decreases while the pass rate continues to drop.  For QA datasets, this inconsistency may be attributed to the inclusion of distracting information, which confuses the model and lowers its confidence, leading to an increase in perplexity.  However, in code datasets, perplexity shows no clear trend and behaves paradoxically with correctness—for example, in the DS1000 dataset, perplexity even decreases as correctness declines.  This inconsistency and the observations in RQ2 suggest that perplexity is not a reliable metric for evaluating code generation quality in LLMs and RAG systems.  Retrieval recall does not determine RAG system performance when the number of documents varies.  In Figure 10, we summarize the retrieval recalls of RAG systems under varying numbers of documents to explore the impact of document numbers.  For QA tasks, correctness initially increases, stabilizes, and then slightly decreases (Figure 8.a\&c), while retrieval recall rises sharply at first, then more gradually (Figure 10.a).  Although the trends for correctness and retrieval recall align at the beginning, they diverge later.  In code tasks, this divergence is even more pronounced: while RAG system correctness initially rises and then declines (Figure 8.b\&d), retrieval recall continues to steadily increase (Figure 10.b).  This suggests that the benefit of higher retrieval recall is offset by other factors when more documents are added, resulting in stable performance in QA tasks and declining accuracy in code tasks.  Adding more documents causes RAG systems to make errors on previous correct instances.  To analyze the side effects of adding more documents, we use RAG systems with the top-5 retrieved documents as the baseline and calculate the percentage of instances correctly solved by the baseline but rendered incorrect as larger numbers of documents are included.  As shown in Figure 11, RAG systems make progressively more mistakes as additional documents are added, particularly in Llama and code tasks.  For every five additional documents, error rates increase by an average of 1% in code tasks and 1.5% in QA tasks using Llama.  While the mistakes made by the RAG system with the top-10 documents, compared to the baseline (top-5) system, may partly result from the inherent instability of LLMs, the steadily increasing error rate demonstrates that including more documents has a clear negative side effect on RAG systems.  The actual impact of this side effect is likely even greater than shown in the figure, as RAG systems with top-15 documents not only make mistakes on instances correctly solved by the top-5 system but also on those correctly handled by the top-10 system and so on.  This degradation is likely caused by the growing presence of distracting information, which confuses LLMs and leads to incorrect answers for problems they could initially solve.  This explains the stabilization or decline in RAG system correctness with increasing document numbers despite the continuous rise in retrieval recall.

Fig.  10: Retrieval recall of RAG systems with varying numbers of documents.  A corresponding decline.  In code tasks, perplexity remains stable or even decreases while the pass rate continues to drop.  For QA datasets, this inconsistency may be attributed to the inclusion of distracting information, which confuses the model and lowers its confidence, leading to an increase in perplexity.  However, in code datasets, perplexity shows no clear trend and behaves paradoxically with correctness—for example, in the DS1000 dataset, perplexity even decreases as correctness declines.  This inconsistency and the observations in RQ2 suggest that perplexity is not a reliable metric for evaluating code generation quality in LLMs and RAG systems.  Retrieval recall does not determine RAG system performance when the number of documents varies.  In Figure 10, we summarize the retrieval recalls of RAG systems under varying numbers of documents to explore the impact of document numbers.  For QA tasks, correctness initially increases, stabilizes, and then slightly decreases (Figure 8.a\&c), while retrieval recall rises sharply at first, then more gradually (Figure 10.a).  Although the trends for correctness and retrieval recall align at the beginning, they diverge later.  In code tasks, this divergence is even more pronounced: while RAG system correctness initially rises and then declines (Figure 8.b\&d), retrieval recall continues to steadily increase (Figure 10.b).  This suggests that the benefit of higher retrieval recall is offset by other factors when more documents are added, resulting in stable performance in QA tasks and declining accuracy in code tasks.  Adding more documents causes RAG systems to make errors on previous correct instances.  To analyze the side effects of adding more documents, we use RAG systems with the top-5 retrieved documents as the baseline and calculate the percentage of instances correctly solved by the baseline but rendered incorrect as larger numbers of documents are included.  As shown in Figure 11, RAG systems make progressively more mistakes as additional documents are added, particularly in Llama and code tasks.  For every five additional documents, error rates increase by an average of 1% in code tasks and 1.5% in QA tasks using Llama.  While the mistakes made by the RAG system with the top-10 documents, compared to the baseline (top-5) system, may partly result from the inherent instability of LLMs, the steadily increasing error rate demonstrates that including more documents has a clear negative side effect on RAG systems.  The actual impact of this side effect is likely even greater than shown in the figure, as RAG systems with top-15 documents not only make mistakes on instances correctly solved by the top-5 system but also on those correctly handled by the top-10 system and so on.  This degradation is likely caused by the growing presence of distracting information, which confuses LLMs and leads to incorrect answers for problems they could initially solve.  This explains the stabilization or decline in RAG system correctness with increasing document numbers despite the continuous rise in retrieval recall.  Based on our findings regarding document selection, we summarize the following guidelines for developers:

* Guideline-6: While effective for QA tasks, perplexity might be unreliable for evaluating code generation due to its poor correlation with code correctness.

In Figure 10, we summarize the retrieval recalls of RAG systems under varying numbers of documents to explore the impact of document numbers. To analyze the side effects of adding more documents, we use RAG systems with the top-5 retrieved documents as the baseline and calculate the percentage of instances correctly solved by the baseline but rendered incorrect as larger numbers of documents are included. This inconsistency and the observations in RQ2 suggest that perplexity is not a reliable metric for evaluating code generation quality in LLMs and RAG systems.  Retrieval recall does not determine RAG system performance when the number of documents varies.  In Figure 10, we summarize the retrieval recalls of RAG systems under varying numbers of documents to explore the impact of document numbers.  For QA tasks, correctness initially increases, stabilizes, and then slightly decreases (Figure 8.a\&c), while retrieval recall rises sharply at first, then more gradually (Figure 10.a). Adding more documents causes RAG systems to make errors on previous correct instances.  To analyze the side effects of adding more documents, we use RAG systems with the top-5 retrieved documents as the baseline and calculate the percentage of instances correctly solved by the baseline but rendered incorrect as larger numbers of documents are included.  As shown in Figure 11, RAG systems make progressively more mistakes as additional documents are added, particularly in Llama and code tasks.  For every five additional documents, error rates increase by an average of 1% in code tasks and 1.5% in QA tasks using Llama.  While the mistakes made by the RAG system with the top-10 documents, compared to the baseline (top-5) system, may partly result from the inherent instability of LLMs, the steadily increasing error rate demonstrates that including more documents has a clear negative side effect on RAG systems.  The actual impact of this side effect is likely even greater than shown in the figure, as RAG systems with top-15 documents not only make mistakes on instances correctly solved by the top-5 system but also on those correctly handled by the top-10 system and so on.  This degradation is likely caused by the growing presence of distracting information, which confuses LLMs and leads to incorrect answers for problems they could initially solve.  This explains the stabilization or decline in RAG system correctness with increasing document numbers despite the continuous rise in retrieval recall.  * Guideline-7: Incorporating more documents degrades RAG system performance, so increase the number only if it significantly enhances retrieval recall.  This effect can be more pronounced in less capable LLMs.

In Figure 10, we summarize the retrieval recalls of RAG systems under varying numbers of documents to explore the impact of document numbers. Adding more documents causes RAG systems to make errors on previous correct instances.  To analyze the side effects of adding more documents, we use RAG systems with the top-5 retrieved documents as the baseline and calculate the percentage of instances correctly solved by the baseline but rendered incorrect as larger numbers of documents are included.  As shown in Figure 11, RAG systems make progressively more mistakes as additional documents are added, particularly in Llama and code tasks.  For every five additional documents, error rates increase by an average of 1% in code tasks and 1.5% in QA tasks using Llama.  While the mistakes made by the RAG system with the top-10 documents, compared to the baseline (top-5) system, may partly result from the inherent instability of LLMs, the steadily increasing error rate demonstrates that including more documents has a clear negative side effect on RAG systems. In code tasks, perplexity remains stable or even decreases while the pass rate continues to drop.  For QA datasets, this inconsistency may be attributed to the inclusion of distracting information, which confuses the model and lowers its confidence, leading to an increase in perplexity.  However, in code datasets, perplexity shows no clear trend and behaves paradoxically with correctness—for example, in the DS1000 dataset, perplexity even decreases as correctness declines.  This inconsistency and the observations in RQ2 suggest that perplexity is not a reliable metric for evaluating code generation quality in LLMs and RAG systems.  Retrieval recall does not determine RAG system performance when the number of documents varies.  In Figure 10, we summarize the retrieval recalls of RAG systems under varying numbers of documents to explore the impact of document numbers.  For QA tasks, correctness initially increases, stabilizes, and then slightly decreases (Figure 8.a\&c), while retrieval recall rises sharply at first, then more gradually (Figure 10.a).  Although the trends for correctness and retrieval recall align at the beginning, they diverge later.  In code tasks, this divergence is even more pronounced: while RAG system correctness initially rises and then declines (Figure 8.b\&d), retrieval recall continues to steadily increase (Figure 10.b).  This suggests that the benefit of higher retrieval recall is offset by other factors when more documents are added, resulting in stable performance in QA tasks and declining accuracy in code tasks.  Adding more documents causes RAG systems to make errors on previous correct instances.  To analyze the side effects of adding more documents, we use RAG systems with the top-5 retrieved documents as the baseline and calculate the percentage of instances correctly solved by the baseline but rendered incorrect as larger numbers of documents are included.  As shown in Figure 11, RAG systems make progressively more mistakes as additional documents are added, particularly in Llama and code tasks.  For every five additional documents, error rates increase by an average of 1% in code tasks and 1.5% in QA tasks using Llama.  While the mistakes made by the RAG system with the top-10 documents, compared to the baseline (top-5) system, may partly result from the inherent instability of LLMs, the steadily increasing error rate demonstrates that including more documents has a clear negative side effect on RAG systems.  The actual impact of this side effect is likely even greater than shown in the figure, as RAG systems with top-15 documents not only make mistakes on instances correctly solved by the top-5 system but also on those correctly handled by the top-10 system and so on.  This degradation is likely caused by the growing presence of distracting information, which confuses LLMs and leads to incorrect answers for problems they could initially solve.  This explains the stabilization or decline in RAG system correctness with increasing document numbers despite the continuous rise in retrieval recall. To analyze the side effects of adding more documents, we use RAG systems with the top-5 retrieved documents as the baseline and calculate the percentage of instances correctly solved by the baseline but rendered incorrect as larger numbers of documents are included.  As shown in Figure 11, RAG systems make progressively more mistakes as additional documents are added, particularly in Llama and code tasks.  For every five additional documents, error rates increase by an average of 1% in code tasks and 1.5% in QA tasks using Llama.  While the mistakes made by the RAG system with the top-10 documents, compared to the baseline (top-5) system, may partly result from the inherent instability of LLMs, the steadily increasing error rate demonstrates that including more documents has a clear negative side effect on RAG systems.  The actual impact of this side effect is likely even greater than shown in the figure, as RAG systems with top-15 documents not only make mistakes on instances correctly solved by the top-5 system but also on those correctly handled by the top-10 system and so on.  This degradation is likely caused by the growing presence of distracting information, which confuses LLMs and leads to incorrect answers for problems they could initially solve.  This explains the stabilization or decline in RAG system correctness with increasing document numbers despite the continuous rise in retrieval recall.  Based on our findings regarding document selection, we summarize the following guidelines for developers:

* Guideline-6: While effective for QA tasks, perplexity might be unreliable for evaluating code generation due to its poor correlation with code correctness.
 * Guideline-7: Incorporating more documents degrades RAG system performance, so increase the number only if it significantly enhances retrieval recall.  This effect can be more pronounced in less capable LLMs.

The actual impact of this side effect is likely even greater than shown in the figure, as RAG systems with top-15 documents not only make mistakes on instances correctly solved by the top-5 system but also on those correctly handled by the top-10 system and so on.  This degradation is likely caused by the growing presence of distracting information, which confuses LLMs and leads to incorrect answers for problems they could initially solve.  | Method           | Description                                                                                    |
| ---------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |

| Least-to-Most    | Break down the problem into sub-problems, then solve each of them to reach the final solution.  |

\# 7.2 Results and Discussions Most prompt techniques fail to improve RAG system correctness.  Comparing the overall results across QA tasks and code tasks (represented by every fourth bar in Figure 12), we find that RAG systems using most prompt techniques underperform relative to our baseline RAG system (employing the prompt discussed in Section 3.4.1, indicated by dashed lines).  In QA tasks, no prompt techniques enhance overall system performance.  Only Self-Consistency and Least-to-Most achieve similar performance to the baseline under GPT-3.5, while no techniques achieve baseline performance under Llama2-13B.  In code tasks, only Few-shot, Least-to-Most, and Self-Refine either match or exceed baseline performance across both models.

The impact of prompt techniques is inconsistent.  Our analysis of prompt techniques across different datasets and models reveals substantial inconsistencies in their effectiveness.  While certain techniques outperform the baseline in specific scenarios, they often underperform in others.  For instance, CoN shows improvement in NQ with GPT-3.5 but fails to deliver comparable results in other QA datasets.  Similarly, Few-shot enhances performance in DS1000 with GPT-3.5 and CoNaLa with Llama yet performs poorly in CoNaLa with GPT-3.5 and DS1000 with Llama.  Additionally, CoT and Self-consistency are effective in PNE with GPT-3.5 but do not yield similar benefits in CoNaLa or DS1000.  This indicates that the effectiveness of prompt techniques is both task- and model-specific, posing challenges for their consistent application in real-world scenarios involving diverse tasks and conversational styles.  Mitigating this issue may require the development of more generalized prompting methods that perform robustly across tasks and models.  Such methods would help avoid scenarios where prompts optimized for one task fail to deliver adequate performance on others, thereby maintaining the overall effectiveness of the system.  System confidence across different prompt techniques is incomparable.

Techniques like Self-Refine produce more intricate responses, increasing perplexity, while simpler techniques like zero-shot lower it.  Thus, perplexity values across prompt techniques are inherently incomparable.  Prompt Techniques have the potential to improve RAG system performance.  Our findings indicate that most prompt techniques fail to enhance overall RAG system performance, a counter-intuitive result that challenges the common belief in their ability.  To explore their potential, we calculate the percentage of instances correctly resolved by RAG systems utilizing advanced prompt techniques but incorrectly resolved by the baseline RAG systems, as shown in Figure 14.  The results reveal that all prompt techniques successfully address a considerable number of instances that the baseline system fails to handle.  Despite overall subpar performance, some techniques exhibit a higher proportion of "only correct instances."  For example, Plan-and-Solve achieves the highest percentage of "only correct instances" in QA tasks despite its low overall correctness.  Similarly, CoT addresses a substantial number of "only correct instances" in code tasks.  These observations indicate that prompt techniques have the potential to outperform the baseline, as they successfully address many "only correct" examples.  However, they also reveal an inefficiency in advanced prompt techniques: they fail to handle straightforward problems that the baseline prompts resolve effectively.  This highlights the trade-offs of advanced techniques, as their inefficiencies in simpler cases can undermine their advantages.  Addressing this ineffectiveness may be a key point in optimizing and tuning prompt techniques for specific tasks and models.  # 8 IMPLICATION AND OPPORTUNITY Optimizing RAG systems.  In this study, we analyzed two critical components of RAG systems—retrieved documents and prompts—focusing on their four key factors.  The study yields valuable insights and results in nine guidelines to support the development and optimization of RAG systems.  While we have made progress toward optimizing RAG systems, the systematic and automated tuning of RAG system settings remains a complex challenge that demands further research and deeper exploration.  Addressing RAG system degradations.  Our study reveals several causes of RAG system degradation, including the negative impact of distracting documents, the gap in fully utilizing oracle documents, the inclusion of excessive information, and the inefficiency of prompt techniques.  Monitoring and addressing these causes is crucial for preventing RAG system performance decline and building reliable, trustworthy LLM-driven RAG systems.

Thus, perplexity values across prompt techniques are inherently incomparable.  Prompt Techniques have the potential to improve RAG system performance.  Our findings indicate that most prompt techniques fail to enhance overall RAG system performance, a counter-intuitive result that challenges the common belief in their ability.  To explore their potential, we calculate the percentage of instances correctly resolved by RAG systems utilizing advanced prompt techniques but incorrectly resolved by the baseline RAG systems, as shown in Figure 14.  The results reveal that all prompt techniques successfully address a considerable number of instances that the baseline system fails to handle.  Despite overall subpar performance, some techniques exhibit a higher proportion of "only correct instances."  For example, Plan-and-Solve achieves the highest percentage of "only correct instances" in QA tasks despite its low overall correctness.  Similarly, CoT addresses a substantial number of "only correct instances" in code tasks.  These observations indicate that prompt techniques have the potential to outperform the baseline, as they successfully address many "only correct" examples.  However, they also reveal an inefficiency in advanced prompt techniques: they fail to handle straightforward problems that the baseline prompts resolve effectively.  This highlights the trade-offs of advanced techniques, as their inefficiencies in simpler cases can undermine their advantages.  Addressing this ineffectiveness may be a key point in optimizing and tuning prompt techniques for specific tasks and models.  # 8 IMPLICATION AND OPPORTUNITY Optimizing RAG systems.  In this study, we analyzed two critical components of RAG systems—retrieved documents and prompts—focusing on their four key factors.  The study yields valuable insights and results in nine guidelines to support the development and optimization of RAG systems.  While we have made progress toward optimizing RAG systems, the systematic and automated tuning of RAG system settings remains a complex challenge that demands further research and deeper exploration.  Addressing RAG system degradations.  Our study reveals several causes of RAG system degradation, including the negative impact of distracting documents, the gap in fully utilizing oracle documents, the inclusion of excessive information, and the inefficiency of prompt techniques.  Monitoring and addressing these causes is crucial for preventing RAG system performance decline and building reliable, trustworthy LLM-driven RAG systems.  Perplexity as a system confidence indicator.  When developing reliable LLM-driven systems, assessing the confidence of model-generated responses is critical.  Our study demonstrates a strong correlation between perplexity and the quality of retrieved documents in QA tasks, highlighting its potential as a useful indicator for monitoring system performance and robustness.  However, perplexity proves unreliable across different prompt techniques or in code-related tasks.  This highlights a pressing need for new confidence evaluation methods designed for diverse prompt techniques and code-related tasks.  The effect of irrelevant documents.  Our empirical study uncovers a surprising finding: irrelevant documents can significantly enhance LLMs’ code generation abilities.  As an initial exploration, we identify specific features and propose that this phenomenon resembles the 'magic word' effect.  In future work, we will further study the underlying mechanisms of this effectiveness and develop methodology to ensure that it can be reliably and ethically leveraged in trustworthy LLM-driven systems.  Retrieval for code tasks.  Retrieval in code tasks differs fundamentally from QA tasks.  While QA tasks often involve retrieving documents that directly contain the required information, retrieval for code tasks provides contextual or structural guidance rather than direct solutions.  This increases the challenge of formally collecting and processing useful knowledge into indexed retrieval databases, and of defining and identifying oracle documents to evaluate retrieval quality.  However, foundational research in these areas remains insufficient.  Moreover, retrieval recall in code-related tasks often lags behind QA contexts.

metadata.window: Addressing this ineffectiveness may be a key point in optimizing and tuning prompt techniques for specific tasks and models.  # 8 IMPLICATION AND OPPORTUNITY Optimizing RAG systems.  In this study, we analyzed two critical components of RAG systems—retrieved documents and prompts—focusing on their four key factors.  The study yields valuable insights and results in nine guidelines to support the development and optimization of RAG systems.  While we have made progress toward optimizing RAG systems, the systematic and automated tuning of RAG system settings remains a complex challenge that demands further research and deeper exploration.  Addressing RAG system degradations.  Our study reveals several causes of RAG system degradation, including the negative impact of distracting documents, the gap in fully utilizing oracle documents, the inclusion of excessive information, and the inefficiency of prompt techniques.  Monitoring and addressing these causes is crucial for preventing RAG system performance decline and building reliable, trustworthy LLM-driven RAG systems.  Perplexity as a system confidence indicator.  When developing reliable LLM-driven systems, assessing the confidence of model-generated responses is critical.  Our study demonstrates a strong correlation between perplexity and the quality of retrieved documents in QA tasks, highlighting its potential as a useful indicator for monitoring system performance and robustness.  However, perplexity proves unreliable across different prompt techniques or in code-related tasks.  This highlights a pressing need for new confidence evaluation methods designed for diverse prompt techniques and code-related tasks.  The effect of irrelevant documents.  Our empirical study uncovers a surprising finding: irrelevant documents can significantly enhance LLMs’ code generation abilities.  As an initial exploration, we identify specific features and propose that this phenomenon resembles the 'magic word' effect.  In future work, we will further study the underlying mechanisms of this effectiveness and develop methodology to ensure that it can be reliably and ethically leveraged in trustworthy LLM-driven systems.  Retrieval for code tasks.  Retrieval in code tasks differs fundamentally from QA tasks.  While QA tasks often involve retrieving documents that directly contain the required information, retrieval for code tasks provides contextual or structural guidance rather than direct solutions.  This increases the challenge of formally collecting and processing useful knowledge into indexed retrieval databases, and of defining and identifying oracle documents to evaluate retrieval quality.  However, foundational research in these areas remains insufficient.  Moreover, retrieval recall in code-related tasks often lags behind QA contexts.  As discussed in Section 3.5, the retrieval recall of the top-100 documents for QA datasets reaches 80% across all three datasets, while for code datasets, it only achieves 40%.  Unsuccessful retrievals, particularly the presence of distracting documents, negatively affect task performance.  This underscores the need for improved retrieval accuracy in code-related tasks—a critical yet under-explored research area.  Optimizing prompts for multi-task scenarios.  Our findings in RQ4 show that simple, generalizable prompts are often more effective as a plug-and-play solution for multi-task RAG systems, whereas complex prompts, though beneficial for specific tasks, can hinder overall performance across diverse tasks.  Despite these challenges, advanced prompt techniques still hold significant potential to improve the performance of LLMs and RAG systems.  Traditionally, prompt engineering has focused on generating outputs for single or narrowly defined tasks.  However, with the increasing demands of LLM-driven applications, the ability to handle multiple diverse tasks has become essential.  This highlights prompt refinement and optimization for multi-task scenarios as an important yet under-explored area of research.

metadata.window: \# 9 RELATED WORK # 9.1 RAG System Performance Analysis Several prior works have investigated how various factors and design choices in RAG systems affect overall performance.  Among them, Liu et al.  \[50] examine the influence of document positioning and found that placing oracle documents in the middle of the prompt leads to inferior performance.  Cuconasu et al.  \[53] analyze the effects of document type and position on RAG system performance, identifying the negative impact of distracting documents and the potential benefits of noise documents.  However, their study is limited to the retrieval phase and focuses solely on a single QA task (NQ).  As discussed in Section 4, our findings regarding the effect of irrelevant documents in code tasks differ from theirs.  Wang et al.  \[60] focus on comparing various design choices in the retrieval phase of RAG systems, such as retrievers and reranking techniques.  In contrast, our controlled experiments provide a deeper understanding of the critical factors related to retrieved documents and their implications for overall system performance.  Barnett et al.  \[61] identify seven failure points in RAG systems through three case studies from a software engineering perspective.  While they highlight challenges in applying RAG systems, they do not delve into how specific factors contribute to these failures or provide guidance on avoiding or mitigating them.  Other works explore different aspects of the RAG system.  Chen et al.  \[62] investigate the implication of retrieval granularity, while Ovadia et al.  \[63] compare the effectiveness of RAG techniques with fine-tuning for knowledge updates.  Xu et al.  \[64] compare the performance of RAG systems with LLMs that have long-context windows, and Chen et al.  \[9] examine the effectiveness of RAG techniques in long-form QA tasks.  # 9.2 System Engineering for AI-enabled Systems Extensive research has explored the distinctive software engineering challenges posed by AI-enabled machine learning systems.

Cuconasu et al.  \[53] analyze the effects of document type and position on RAG system performance, identifying the negative impact of distracting documents and the potential benefits of noise documents.  However, their study is limited to the retrieval phase and focuses solely on a single QA task (NQ).  As discussed in Section 4, our findings regarding the effect of irrelevant documents in code tasks differ from theirs.  Wang et al.  \[60] focus on comparing various design choices in the retrieval phase of RAG systems, such as retrievers and reranking techniques.  In contrast, our controlled experiments provide a deeper understanding of the critical factors related to retrieved documents and their implications for overall system performance.  Barnett et al.  \[61] identify seven failure points in RAG systems through three case studies from a software engineering perspective.  While they highlight challenges in applying RAG systems, they do not delve into how specific factors contribute to these failures or provide guidance on avoiding or mitigating them.  Other works explore different aspects of the RAG system.  Chen et al.  \[62] investigate the implication of retrieval granularity, while Ovadia et al.  \[63] compare the effectiveness of RAG techniques with fine-tuning for knowledge updates.  Xu et al.  \[64] compare the performance of RAG systems with LLMs that have long-context windows, and Chen et al.  \[9] examine the effectiveness of RAG techniques in long-form QA tasks.  # 9.2 System Engineering for AI-enabled Systems Extensive research has explored the distinctive software engineering challenges posed by AI-enabled machine learning systems.  Several studies highlight critical engineering challenges in AI-enabled systems, including design risks, security requirements, and integration issues across development, production, and organizational contexts — essential considerations for building robust and reliable AI systems \[65]–\[67].

Cuconasu et al.  \[53] analyze the effects of document type and position on RAG system performance, identifying the negative impact of distracting documents and the potential benefits of noise documents.  However, their study is limited to the retrieval phase and focuses solely on a single QA task (NQ).  As discussed in Section 4, our findings regarding the effect of irrelevant documents in code tasks differ from theirs.  Wang et al.  \[60] focus on comparing various design choices in the retrieval phase of RAG systems, such as retrievers and reranking techniques.  In contrast, our controlled experiments provide a deeper understanding of the critical factors related to retrieved documents and their implications for overall system performance.  Barnett et al.  \[61] identify seven failure points in RAG systems through three case studies from a software engineering perspective.  While they highlight challenges in applying RAG systems, they do not delve into how specific factors contribute to these failures or provide guidance on avoiding or mitigating them.  Other works explore different aspects of the RAG system.  Chen et al.  \[62] investigate the implication of retrieval granularity, while Ovadia et al.  \[63] compare the effectiveness of RAG techniques with fine-tuning for knowledge updates.  Xu et al.  \[64] compare the performance of RAG systems with LLMs that have long-context windows, and Chen et al.  \[9] examine the effectiveness of RAG techniques in long-form QA tasks.  # 9.2 System Engineering for AI-enabled Systems Extensive research has explored the distinctive software engineering challenges posed by AI-enabled machine learning systems.  Several studies highlight critical engineering challenges in AI-enabled systems, including design risks, security requirements, and integration issues across development, production, and organizational contexts — essential considerations for building robust and reliable AI systems \[65]–\[67].  To address these challenges, a substantial body of work focuses on the development phase of AI models, specifically on testing the reliability and robustness of standalone deep learning models (DNN) at the unit level \[68].  For instance, various DNN-specific coverage criteria have been proposed to guide the testing and enhance the understanding of DNN behavior \[69]–\[71].  Building on these foundations, techniques for synthesizing test inputs have been developed to support comprehensive DNN testing \[72]–\[74].  Other work aims to improve the quality of DNNs through testing on its components, including training and testing data \[75]–\[78], as well as DL libraries \[79]–\[81].  Beyond model-specific testing, researchers have explored testing approaches for entire AI-enabled software at the system level.  This includes testing autonomous driving systems \[82]–\[96], machine translation systems \[97]–\[100] and applications leveraging cloud-based machine learning APIs \[101], \[102].  Additionally, empirical studies offer insights into the software engineering challenges faced by real-world AI applications.  For example, several works categorize and analyze common bugs found in AI-enabled applications \[103]–\[105].  Case studies further explore and address the development challenges of building and integrating AI systems \[106], \[107].  Finally, a range of studies investigates the deployment challenges involved in deploying and maintaining ML/DL models \[108]–\[110].  While previous works have analyzed and addressed challenges in AI-enabled systems, their methodologies are not directly applicable to LLM-driven RAG systems.  On the one hand, LLMs, as the core of the systems we studied, operate on fundamentally different principles from traditional classification DNNs.  Unlike them, LLMs generate free-form outputs, resulting in exponentially larger behavioral spaces.  The complexity increases further in RAG systems, which integrate external databases containing diverse data types such as text, audio, or images.

Several studies highlight critical engineering challenges in AI-enabled systems, including design risks, security requirements, and integration issues across development, production, and organizational contexts — essential considerations for building robust and reliable AI systems \[65]–\[67].  To address these challenges, a substantial body of work focuses on the development phase of AI models, specifically on testing the reliability and robustness of standalone deep learning models (DNN) at the unit level \[68].  For instance, various DNN-specific coverage criteria have been proposed to guide the testing and enhance the understanding of DNN behavior \[69]–\[71].  Building on these foundations, techniques for synthesizing test inputs have been developed to support comprehensive DNN testing \[72]–\[74].  Other work aims to improve the quality of DNNs through testing on its components, including training and testing data \[75]–\[78], as well as DL libraries \[79]–\[81].  Beyond model-specific testing, researchers have explored testing approaches for entire AI-enabled software at the system level.  This includes testing autonomous driving systems \[82]–\[96], machine translation systems \[97]–\[100] and applications leveraging cloud-based machine learning APIs \[101], \[102].  Additionally, empirical studies offer insights into the software engineering challenges faced by real-world AI applications.  For example, several works categorize and analyze common bugs found in AI-enabled applications \[103]–\[105].  Case studies further explore and address the development challenges of building and integrating AI systems \[106], \[107].  Finally, a range of studies investigates the deployment challenges involved in deploying and maintaining ML/DL models \[108]–\[110].  While previous works have analyzed and addressed challenges in AI-enabled systems, their methodologies are not directly applicable to LLM-driven RAG systems.  On the one hand, LLMs, as the core of the systems we studied, operate on fundamentally different principles from traditional classification DNNs.  Unlike them, LLMs generate free-form outputs, resulting in exponentially larger behavioral spaces.  The complexity increases further in RAG systems, which integrate external databases containing diverse data types such as text, audio, or images.  Additionally, while traditional AI modules are typically task-specific, LLM-driven RAG systems are highly versatile and capable of supporting a broad range of applications.  On the other hand, development and deployment patterns for RAG systems differ significantly from those of traditional ML systems.  LLMs, as extremely large models, are challenging to develop independently and rely heavily on robust infrastructure.  This shift introduces new challenges in system engineering to LLM-driven RAG systems. metadata.window: To address these challenges, a substantial body of work focuses on the development phase of AI models, specifically on testing the reliability and robustness of standalone deep learning models (DNN) at the unit level \[68].  For instance, various DNN-specific coverage criteria have been proposed to guide the testing and enhance the understanding of DNN behavior \[69]–\[71].  Building on these foundations, techniques for synthesizing test inputs have been developed to support comprehensive DNN testing \[72]–\[74].  Other work aims to improve the quality of DNNs through testing on its components, including training and testing data \[75]–\[78], as well as DL libraries \[79]–\[81].  Beyond model-specific testing, researchers have explored testing approaches for entire AI-enabled software at the system level.  This includes testing autonomous driving systems \[82]–\[96], machine translation systems \[97]–\[100] and applications leveraging cloud-based machine learning APIs \[101], \[102].  Additionally, empirical studies offer insights into the software engineering challenges faced by real-world AI applications.  For example, several works categorize and analyze common bugs found in AI-enabled applications \[103]–\[105].  Case studies further explore and address the development challenges of building and integrating AI systems \[106], \[107].  Finally, a range of studies investigates the deployment challenges involved in deploying and maintaining ML/DL models \[108]–\[110].  While previous works have analyzed and addressed challenges in AI-enabled systems, their methodologies are not directly applicable to LLM-driven RAG systems.  On the one hand, LLMs, as the core of the systems we studied, operate on fundamentally different principles from traditional classification DNNs.  Unlike them, LLMs generate free-form outputs, resulting in exponentially larger behavioral spaces.  The complexity increases further in RAG systems, which integrate external databases containing diverse data types such as text, audio, or images.  Additionally, while traditional AI modules are typically task-specific, LLM-driven RAG systems are highly versatile and capable of supporting a broad range of applications.  On the other hand, development and deployment patterns for RAG systems differ significantly from those of traditional ML systems.  LLMs, as extremely large models, are challenging to develop independently and rely heavily on robust infrastructure.  This shift introduces new challenges in system engineering to LLM-driven RAG systems.  These differences highlight the unique system engineering challenges posed by RAG systems, necessitating novel approaches for their design, deployment, and maintenance.  # 10 THREATS TO VALIDITY **External Validity. ** The choice of retriever poses a potential threat to the generalizability of our findings.  In this study, we exclusively rely on retrieval results from text-embedding-3-small due to the extensive experiments conducted.  Consequently, the behavior of RAG systems may differ when employing alternative retrievers.  Nevertheless, the variations introduced by different retrievers primarily affect the levels of distracting and oracle documents, which are examined in RQ 1&2, alleviating this concern.  **Internal Validity. ** Our focus on a typical RAG architecture introduces a potential limitation to the internal validity of our findings.  As illustrated in \[16], numerous advanced RAG techniques and architectures exist.  However, these techniques, such as reranking, rewriting, and iterative retrieval, are primarily designed to improve either the quality of retrieved documents or prompts.  Since our analyses directly target these two core components of the RAG system, our findings and guidelines remain relevant and applicable to advanced RAG systems.  # 11 CONCLUSION In this paper, we conducted an in-depth analysis of the development of LLM-driven RAG systems by investigating the impact of retrieved documents and prompts across six datasets spanning NLP and software engineering domains with two models. \# Towards Understanding Retrieval Accuracy and Prompt Quality in RAG Systems Shengming Zhao, Yuheng Huang, Jiayang Song, Zhijie Wang, Chengcheng Wan, Lei Ma Abstract—Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is a pivotal technique for enhancing the capability of large language models (LLMs) and has demonstrated promising efficacy across a diverse spectrum of tasks. While LLM-driven RAG systems show superior performance, they face unique challenges in stability and reliability. Their complexity hinders developers’ efforts to design, maintain, and optimize effective RAG systems. Therefore, it is crucial to understand how RAG’s performance is impacted by its design. In this work, we conduct an early exploratory study toward a better understanding of the mechanism of RAG systems, covering three code datasets, three QA datasets, and two LLMs. We focus on four design factors: retrieval document type, retrieval recall, document selection, and prompt techniques. Our study uncovers how each factor impacts system correctness and confidence, providing valuable insights for developing an accurate and reliable RAG system. Based on these findings, we present nine actionable guidelines for detecting defects and optimizing the performance of RAG systems. We hope our early exploration can inspire further advancements in engineering, improving and maintaining LLM-driven intelligent software systems for greater efficiency and reliability. Index Terms—Large Language Models, LLM, Retrieval Augmented Generation, RAG, System Diagnostics, Software Reliability ✦ # 1 INTRODUCTION Advancements in natural language processing (NLP) have brought Large Language Models (LLMs) \[1]–\[3] to the forefront, revolutionizing both academic research and practical applications across diverse domains. Recently, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) \[4], as a typical and representative LLM-enabled system, has emerged to further enhance the capabilities of LLMs. By retrieving relevant and up-to-date information from external knowledge bases, RAG effectively mitigates key limitations of standalone LLMs, such as the high cost of training and fine-tuning \[3], the phenomenon of hallucination \[5], and inherent input window limitations \[6]. Given its promising performance and cost-effectiveness, RAG has achieved success across various tasks and scenarios, including chatbots \[7], factual QA \[8], long-form generation \[9], and automatic code completion \[10]–\[13]. Moreover, RAG has already become a foundational technology in various real-world products like Contextual AI \[14] and Cohere \[15]. Although the RAG technique has strong potential across various tasks, maximizing its effectiveness is neither straightforward nor consistently guaranteed. Unlike standalone LLMs that rely on fine-tuning, LLM-driven RAG systems require huge integration efforts and careful optimization to achieve high performance, and their effectiveness varies on a case-by-case basis. We highlight the typical workflow of a typical RAG system \[16] into two phases, as shown in Figure 1: (1) the retrieval phase takes the user input query and uses a retriever to search for relevant information from an indexed database, which are retrieved documents; (2) the generation phase uses a prompt generator to create a prompt with retrieved documents and the query, and passes it to a frozen LLM to obtain the final answer. While seemingly straightforward, the LLM-driven RAG system involves sophisticated implementations, with numerous design choices in its pipeline that significantly impact overall system performance. For instance, there are various candidate retrievers \[17]–\[20], as well as advanced retrieval techniques such as reranking \[21], rewriting \[22], iterative retrieving \[23], \[24], that could be employed. Yet, there is a lack of understanding of their effects on system performance, whether they should be adopted, and the concrete scenarios that one technique is better than the others. Therefore, it is hard to diagnose the performance issues of the retrieval phase. By analyzing the impact of these four factors, we uncovered several intriguing and counter-intuitive findings regarding the development of RAG systems: # Retrieval Document Type Analysis In this study, we consider three different types of retrieved documents: oracle (ground-truth), distracting (high similarity but actually useless), and irrelevant (low similarity and lack useful information). Our experiment results reveal that distracting documents negatively impact system performance, and surprisingly, irrelevant documents are more effective than oracle documents in code generation tasks in some cases. Further analysis reveals that irrelevant documents enhance the LLMs’ code generation ability across all scenarios, resulting in an up to 15.6% pass rate increase on average. We also observed an intriguing effect of irrelevant documents, which we termed the “magic word” effect. This effect does not scale with prompt length and is most effective when irrelevant documents are used alone, with a specific type of document diff consistently yielding the greatest improvement. # Retrieval Recall Analysis Although Retrieval recall strongly correlates with RAG system performance, the level of recall required to match the performance of standalone LLMs varies significantly across models and datasets — from as low as 20% to as high as 100%. Further analysis reveals a performance degradation in RAG systems — RAG systems with perfect retrieval recall still fail on a significant proportion of instances where standalone LLMs succeed. We also observed that higher LLM confidence (perplexity) aligned with higher retrieval recall in QA datasets, making the former a useful on-the-fly indicator to predict the latter. # Document Selection Analysis The number of retrieved documents can directly influence the amount of information in the LLM prompt. Our study results reveal that while adding more documents could include more useful information in the prompt, it could also raise error rates on previously correct samples, especially in code tasks and with less powerful LLMs. Moreover, model confidence does not

align with the quality of LLM generation on code problems. Prompt Techniques Analysis. We found that the effectiveness of prompting techniques is highly context-specific when impacting the performance of LLM-driven RAG systems, varying across different models and tasks. While prompt techniques show potential to improve system performance, most of them do not perform better than plain zero-shot prompt in overall effectiveness. In summary, this paper makes the following contributions:

* We analyzed the impact of retrieved documents, providing a quantitative assessment of their impacts on RAG system performance.
* We explored two key design choices in prompt construction for RAG systems, offering valuable guidelines for effective implementation.
* We investigated performance degradations in RAG systems, providing insights into their causes and prevention.
* We established that model confidence serves as an effective metric for QA tasks but proves unreliable in code tasks.
* We explored RAG for code-related tasks, revealing the unique effectiveness of irrelevant documents in enhancing code generation.

\# Contribution to the Software Engineering Field: With rapid progress and adoption, LLM-driven RAG systems have the potential to become significant and representative software systems, with many potential industrial applications. However, RAG, from both concepts and engineering practices, introduces numerous challenges that remain unexplored, with existing studies offering limited understanding and insights. In this paper, our study of LLM-driven RAG system design offers the first exploratory understanding of the engineering challenges and how inadequate design choices degrade the system performance. We uncovered the impact of retrieval recall, retrieval document types, and other aspects on the overall system performance. Based on it, we proposed various tentative solution candidates for practitioners to design, develop, evaluate, and optimize LLM-driven RAG systems from the perspective of system integration. These solutions may guide developers in making correct design choices, including prompts prioritization for improving stability in multi-task RAG systems, confidence-guided LLM inference feedback for improving QA task performance, and many other automated solutions. We also studied RAG performance on code tasks under various settings, providing guidance for LLMs for code. We discovered the unique and significant impact of irrelevant documents and demonstrated the limitations of model confidence in evaluating code-related tasks. # 2 BACKGROUND In this section, we provide an overview of the retrieval and generation phases in RAG systems, detailing their design and implementation. # 2.1 Retrieval Phase As illustrated in Figure 1, the retrieval phase of a LLM-driven RAG system often contains two main components: the indexed database and the retriever. The indexed database is a structured collection of documents D1, D2, . . . , Dn, containing domain knowledge and information related to potential user queries. Organized and optimized for efficient searching, it serves as the foundation for retrieving pertinent information. The retriever ranks all documents in the indexed database based on their similarity to a query. Given a query Q and the indexed database comprising n documents D1, D2, . . . , Dn, the retriever identifies the order of these documents according to a similarity criterion sim. Formally, {Di₁, Di₂, . . . , Diₙ} = sort({D1, D2, . . . , Dn}, sim(Q, Di)) (1) There are two primary types of retrievers, based on their utilization of the sparse or dense representations of queries and documents \[33]. Sparse retrievers compute similarity by projecting the query and documents into a sparse vector space that aligns with the vocabulary of the documents, typically using traditional Bag-of-Words methods such as TF-IDF or BM25 \[17]. To overcome the limitations of these methods, which may struggle with synonyms or varying contextual meanings, dense retrievers \[18], \[19] obtain similarity scores by encoding queries and documents as dense vectors that capture their semantic meaning. # 2.2 Generation Phase The generation phase contains two components: the prompt generator and the frozen LLM. A straightforward implementation of the prompt generator is to concatenate the documents and the query in a simple sequence, represented as < D1, D2, . . . , Dk, P > . Additionally, more sophisticated strategies may include applying various prompt techniques \[27], \[29], \[31], \[32] to better align the prompt with the LLM’s capabilities, or using iterative methods that involve multiple rounds of retrieval and generation \[23], \[24]. The frozen LLM is an off-the-shelf LLM used without modification; therefore, this paper does not focus on it. # 3 STUDY DESIGN This section, we introduce our study design, including datasets, evaluation metrics, retrieval methods, and model settings. Following this, we present the two preliminary studies conducted. # 3.1 Datasets We conduct our study on six representative datasets covering scenarios in both software engineering (SE) and natural language processing (NLP) domains, as listed in Table 1. In the SE domain, automatic code generation and completion are critical tasks \[39] and are considered core capabilities of LLMs \[1], \[3], \[40], \[41]. In this study, we select three Python library-oriented datasets: CoNaLa \[34], DS1000 \[35] and Pandas Numpy Eval(PNE) \[12], since their primary retrieved documents are API documentation \[10], \[42], allowing for well-defined and accessible oracle (ground-truth).
